[Hacker News — orchidfiles.com]
This post will focus mainly on Composer 2.5 in Cursor. These problems may not be present in opus-5.5 or gpt-6.1-sol-pro-max-ultra-thinking-fast. But gpt-6.1-luna, for example, has all the problems listed here. I’ve also encountered many of these problems before in gpt-5.5 and opus-4.6. I don’t know whether they’re present in the newer AI models released recently.

For comparison, let’s take two $20 subscriptions, one for GPT and one for Cursor. With gpt-6.1-sol, my 5-hour limit runs out after just a few requests. If I ask it to change a couple of lines in a readme file, that uses up 10% of the limit. If I ask it to change something in a large codebase, the entire limit gets used up just reading dozens of files, without writing a single line of code.

But GPT also offers a $100 plan with five times the usage limits. And how long would that last me? I work with complex monorepo projects. To make changes to one service, the agent has to read dozens of files in other services and several skills. If the $20 plan runs out after reading 20 files, will the $100 plan run out after reading 100 files?

That’s why I don’t use Sol, but use Luna instead. But it’s very slow. Compared to Composer 2.5, it’s dozens of times slower.

That’s why I don’t use GPT Luna, but use Composer 2.5 instead. It’s very fast and very cheap. And in exchange for that speed and savings, I end up wasting my time and getting stressed out. I’ve encountered some of these problems in Deepseek and other open models. Some models have certain problems but not others. The number and frequency of problems vary even when using the same model, depending on the phase of the moon.

Below is a list of problems I’ve encountered over 100+ hours of working with Composer in Cursor.

The agent writes code and changes dozens of files. I start reviewing the code, and the following conversation ensues:

And I still never got an answer to the question of why that function was needed.

Now, whenever I want to ask it something, I have to turn off agent mode or explicitly tell it not to delete anything. But when I forget to do that, it starts deleting parts of the code in response to a simple question.

Sometimes I spend a lot of time reviewing the code and ask it to change just one function. It changes all the files that have already been reviewed. And these changes don’t even relate to that function.

It might even delete all the work done in this chat. And not just in this one. I ask it to make a commit, and it finds changes to other files mixed in. And it just deletes them. Even though that work was done in other chats.

Also, if I ask it to refactor the code — for example, to rename a method in 50 files — it might delete all the comments it finds in those files. Which has absolutely nothing to do with refactoring the method.

And yet, it doesn’t delete what I ask it to delete. When changing a method’s name, it leaves the old method in place and adds a new one with the new name. That’s its entire refactoring process — so it doesn’t have to change all the files where the old method was called. It’ll simply mark the old method as deprecated and leave it accessible. If I point this out, it will finally do the refactoring, but leave the old method name in the tests and documentation. The tests will fail, and it will say the task is complete and the method has been refactored, but the tests are failing. As far as the agent is concerned, failing tests don’t count as evidence that the task is incomplete.

Also, while working on a task, it might remove an important parameter from the config or from a method that has nothing to do with the task at all. When asked why it removed the parameter, the agent claims it didn’t remove anything. You have to explicitly ask it to check the git diff, because it won’t think to do that on its own.

I already have a working service that listens for events, then updates values in the database and writes them to Redis. I ask the agent to do exactly the same thing in another service.

It does it, but forgets to write to Redis. Or it doesn’t update the values in the database. Or it names files and classes completely differently. Or it puts interfaces and types in the wrong places. After that, it says everything is done. I ask it to check everything it’s done. It checks and once again insists that everything is done. And, of course, all the tests are green, which confirms its conclusion that everything is done. I have to go through many rounds, pointing out each mistake so it can fix it. While fixing one mistake, it introduces new ones.

I ask it again to go through the code and make sure everything matches the other service. It changes a lot of files and says everything is done. I open the first file and see that it’s all wrong. I write to it again, and it replies that everything is done. I open the next file, and it’s the same story. What’s more, I can even point out specific functions in a single file and explain how they differ from the refe

[Hacker News — perplexity.ai]
Perplexity teammates coordinate AI agents, manage ongoing projects, and follow through across ops, marketing, and more.

Perplexity pioneered the first web-capable AI assistant in July 2025 in the Comet browser . It was useful for booking restaurants, shopping, and dozens of uses popular with personal agents today.

Since then, model capabilities have advanced dramatically. And Perplexity Computer is where millions of people and companies do serious work with accurate AI. Personal agents need to be purpose-built for work.

Today, we’re launching teammates, personal agents that can take on that long-running work. They plan and coordinate projects, switch gears as priorities change, and present results for review. Users can inspect and guide their work along the way.

Computer can handle complex projects, but setting up an agent to own ongoing work required planning. Teammates build on the power of Computer, and work inside Computer with all of your tools and files.

A teammate coordinates Computer sessions and other teammates to keep projects moving. They remember and learn as they work across different workstreams like marketing, sales, support, operations, or finance.

Teammates represent a new way of working with AI. Users can delegate ongoing actions to teammates so people can focus on outcomes rather than coordinating every task. Built on Perplexity’s focus on accuracy and Computer’s multi-model capabilities, teammates plan the work, check results along the way, and bring completed work back for review.

Teammates can investigate issues, research a market, or test improvements to a product, among other tasks. They remember project goals, task history, and shared files across runs. Each new task a teammate takes on builds on the work already done.

Teammates monitor ongoing work and follow up as things change. They investigate and act without waiting for a fresh query.

For example, a sales teammate notices when a regular customer stops transacting. The teammate reviews their order history and support issues and investigates what changed.

Then, it creates an offer relevant to that customer or flags any issues to resolve before reaching out. It shares progress updates and approval requests until it completes the work.

Teammates also remember past work and apply feedback to future tasks. If a user tells an operations teammate an agency needs two weeks’ notice, it factors that lead time into future project schedules.

Teammates can work across teams. Add a teammate to a Slack channel and colleagues can hand it work or ask for updates on a task.

Teammates can also pass work to each other. One teammate finds bugs on a website and passes its findings along to another to prepare fixes.

Teammates build on the projects , skills, and memory already available in Computer. For example, a sales teammate can use a project’s existing account research and sales goals, follow a skill for writing outreach, and run a weekly automation to review the pipeline.

It brings those pieces together to identify stalled conversations, prepare follow-ups for review, and apply the results to the next week’s work.

Teammates build on Computer’s existing tool and project permissions. Each teammate runs in a separate environment, with browser sessions separate from other teammates.

Saved credentials are encrypted and entered securely. Users can review completed work, take over the desktop, or redirect a teammate as it works.

Teammates handle ongoing work across business functions. These examples show how monitoring, investigation, and follow-through work together:

Teammates are initially launching on the web and soon on iOS for Perplexity Max subscribers. Free and Pro subscribers can upgrade in Settings > Account > Subscription.

We’ll be expanding teammates’ access and features in the coming weeks.

Perplexity is taking on OpenAI and Anthropic with its own work-focused AI agents. The startup’s new always-on “Teammates” can take on multiple roles within a workspace, while pulling existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools you already use.

Teammates integrate with Perplexity Computer , an AI system that can deploy agents on your device to complete tasks. But Perplexity says Teammates “build on top” of Computer by offering the ability to collaborate and complete “ongoing, large-scale work.” You can assign each Teammate different jobs that they can perform simultaneously — much like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet . Perplexity’s take on the feature is much more expensive, however, as it requires a subscription to its $200 / month Max plan.

Perplexity notes that you can keep tabs on Teammates’ progress through individual threads in the Perplexity app, as well as interact with them in Slack. “Over time, we envision every org having hundreds of teammates working for each person,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas says on X .
